clinicalPearls: A milder allelic variant of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome caused by WAS gene mutations that retain some residual WASP function
The hallmark is microthrombocytopenia: a low platelet count with characteristically small platelets (reduced mean platelet volume)
Immunodeficiency and eczema are absent or mild compared with classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Small platelet size on the film and by automated indices is a key diagnostic pointer distinguishing it from other inherited thrombocytopenias
Despite the milder phenotype, patients remain at risk of significant bleeding and can develop autoimmune complications over time
There is an increased long-term risk of autoimmunity and, less commonly, malignancy, so ongoing follow-up is required
Splenectomy raises platelet counts but increases infection risk and is used cautiously
Diagnosis is confirmed by WAS gene sequencing and assessment of WASP expression
reference.pathophysiology: The WAS gene encodes WASP, a cytoskeletal regulator expressed in haematopoietic cells that links signalling to actin polymerisation. Mutations preserving partial WASP function cause the milder X-linked thrombocytopenia phenotype, whereas null mutations produce classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Impaired cytoskeletal dynamics disturb platelet formation and lead to production of small, structurally abnormal platelets that are also removed prematurely, giving microthrombocytopenia. Residual immune-cell dysfunction predisposes to autoimmunity, and reduced immune surveillance contributes to a smaller malignancy risk.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited thrombocytopenias with normal or large platelets
X-linked neutropenia from activating WAS mutations
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with mean platelet volume and film confirming small platelets
WAS gene sequencing and evaluation of WASP protein expression
Immunological assessment (immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets) to gauge any immune component
Bone marrow examination where the diagnosis is unclear
Autoimmune screen given the predisposition to autoimmunity
Assessment of potential related stem-cell donors when transplant is considered
redFlags: Severe or life-threatening bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage
Development of autoimmune cytopenias or other autoimmune disease
Features suggesting progression toward a more severe Wiskott-Aldrich phenotype or malignancy
Recurrent or unusual infections indicating significant immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: The milder phenotype generally carries a better outlook than classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, but lifelong surveillance is needed because bleeding, autoimmunity, and a smaller malignancy risk persist; allogeneic transplantation is curative and considered in more severe cases.
pitfalls: Diagnosing chronic immune thrombocytopenia and missing the small platelet size that signals a WAS variant
Assuming a benign course and omitting surveillance for autoimmunity and malignancy
Overlooking subtle immune dysfunction in an apparently isolated thrombocytopenia
Performing splenectomy without weighing the added infection risk in a WAS-spectrum disorder
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Platelet transfusion reserved for significant bleeding or surgical cover rather than routine use
Avoidance of antiplatelet drugs and other agents that worsen the bleeding tendency
Immunosuppressive treatment of autoimmune complications as they arise
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is curative and considered in more severe or complicated cases
Long-term surveillance for autoimmunity and for the smaller malignancy risk
Monitoring of platelet count and clinical bleeding, noting the characteristic small platelet size
Genetic counselling with WAS testing and assessment of potential related stem-cell donors
